MSME Form 1 for April to September 2026 is due on 31 October. No extension has been announced.

Who files: companies that buy from micro or small enterprises and have payments pending to them for more than 45 days from acceptance. LLPs and firms don't file, and no nil return is needed.

Keep ready: supplier name, PAN and Udyam number, invoice and acceptance dates, credit terms, payment dates and ageing, the amount unpaid on 30 September, and the reason for each delay.

If you don't file: a penalty of ₹20,000 plus ₹1,000 for every day of delay, up to ₹3 lakh, under section 405(4). It applies to the company and to each officer in default.

The bigger cost is the late payment itself: compound interest at three times the RBI bank rate under the MSMED Act, and the expense disallowed under section 43B(h) until you pay.

GST officers took ₹47,45,000 in cash from his home in November 2022. Nearly four years later, the High Court ordered it returned, with interest.

Why? Section 67(2) of the CGST Act lets officers seize goods, documents, books and things. Money is not "goods" under section 2(52). The tax dispute on his stock continues separately in appeal.

If officers visit: get the cash listed separately in the panchnama with whose it is, keep proof of where it came from, and ask for its release in writing.

Is every rupee credited to your bank account your income? The Income Tax department added up all his bank credits and called ₹13,39,14,241 "hidden turnover".

Loans, transfers between his own accounts and refunds were all treated as sales. When he asked how the figure was worked out, no working was shared, and the final order added three new allegations that were not in the notice.

The Karnataka High Court called it a roving enquiry and set aside the section 148A(3) order, the approval and the reopening notice. The matter goes back for a fresh hearing with the working shared.

Got a 148A notice? Ask for the computation and the material relied on, and keep every bank credit tagged: sales, loan, own transfer, refund.

Got an ITC mismatch demand, but nobody showed you how it was worked out?

A Maharashtra taxpayer faced exactly this. The mismatch chart, the invoice-wise working behind the demand, was not given to him during adjudication, and the first appeal was decided without a proper hearing. The chart was uploaded on the portal only on 6 October 2026, after the orders were passed.

The GST Appellate Tribunal, Thane State Bench, called it a gross violation of natural justice, set aside both orders and sent the matter back for fresh adjudication, preferably within three months.

170 km on the e-way bill. 800 km on the road.

A transporter was moving a vehicle chassis from Udham Singh Nagar to Ghazipur, about 800 km. The e-way bill auto-recorded the distance as 170 km, so it expired mid-route. Officers seized the goods and imposed a penalty of Rs 30,63,680 under section 129(3), even though the invoice and every document were in order.

The Allahabad High Court quashed the penalty: the expiry came from the auto-filled distance, not from any intent to evade tax.

Before every dispatch: check the distance on the e-way bill, note the validity end time, extend validity before it lapses if you're running late, and keep the invoice and e-way bill with the driver.

Case: Metropolis Logistics Pvt Ltd v. Additional Commissioner, Allahabad High Court (reported October 2026).

Buying Diwali gifts for your team and clients? Check these three numbers first.

₹15,000: what an employee can get in gifts and vouchers tax-free in a year (it was ₹5,000 till March 2026). Cross it and the whole amount is taxed as salary.

₹50,000: gifts to an employee up to this value in a year stay outside GST. Input tax credit on gifts is still blocked.

₹20,000: gifts to one client or dealer above this in a year need 10% TDS before you hand them over.

Cash, gift cheques and the Diwali bonus are taxed as salary, whatever the amount.

One cousin won't sign, and your share of the family land is stuck at the registry. In Maharashtra, there is now a way forward.
